title: How Career Services & Admissions Can Work Together on Career Outcomes
summary: Learn how Career Services can give Admissions accurate career outcomes and support information, set realistic expectations for prospective students, and create a smoother transition into career preparation once students enroll.
body_markdown:
If your career center is supporting Admissions with career outcomes, employer information, or descriptions of career support, the key is consistency.


Prospective students should hear an accurate picture of what career services offers before enrollment, understand what will be expected of them, and encounter the same experience once they arrive.


This guide explains what career services teams should provide to Admissions, how career outcomes and support should be communicated, and how the two teams can create a smoother handoff from recruitment to enrollment.


Stage What Career Services should do


Prospective student Give Admissions accurate outcome data, context, and service information


Admitted student Help Admissions explain what career preparation will involve


Pre-arrival Introduce a small number of useful career actions and expectations


First term Give students a clear entry point into Career Services


## What Career Information Should Career Services Give Admissions?


Career services should give Admissions a defined set of approved career outcomes, service information, and student expectations that can be used consistently across recruitment conversations.


For outcomes, that may include:


- employment and continuing-education rates
- internship participation
- common industries and employers
- [salary data](https://www.hiration.com/blog/salary-data-career-advising-higher-ed/) where appropriate
- graduate-school destinations
- program-level outcomes where sufficient data exists


The numbers alone are not enough.


Career services should also provide the context Admissions needs to interpret them correctly.


For example, an outcome rate should make clear which graduating class it represents, what population is included, how the outcome is defined, and what data source supports it.


Employer names should be presented as actual destinations rather than implied opportunities available to every student.


Admissions also needs a clear description of the support students can access.


That may include career exploration,[resume support](https://www.hiration.com/blog/resume-critique-rubric-career-centers-higher-ed/) , interview preparation, employer events, job-search resources, digital tools, and individual advising.


A shared reference can keep this information consistent.


Information What Career Services should provide


Outcome rates Figure, definition, reporting period, population, and source


Salary data Population represented and measure being reported


Employer examples Verified destinations with appropriate context


Career services Current resources students can actually access


Recruiting timelines Important timelines students should understand early


Student expectations What students will need to do themselves


The aim is not to review every admissions message. It is to give Admissions a reliable source of career information that is difficult to misinterpret.


Career Services + Admissions: Clear Roles, Shared Outcomes


## How Can Career Services Help Admissions Describe Career Support Accurately?


Career Services should help Admissions explain what support students can access, how that support works, and what students are expected to do themselves.


The message should focus on the career-development experience rather than implying that Career Services produces a particular job, salary, employer, or internship.


Prospective students should be able to understand:


- what career resources they will have access to
- when they can start using them
- how Career Services supports exploration and preparation
- which services are self-service, advisor-led, or both
- what students are expected to do themselves
- which outcomes the institution can report but cannot promise


For example, Career Services may want Admissions to avoid broad language such as:


*“Our Career Center helps students get jobs.”*


A more accurate explanation would be:


*“Students have access to career exploration, application preparation, interview support, employer programming, and individual advising throughout their time here.”*


That describes what the institution actually provides.


Career Services should also help Admissions set expectations around student participation.


Students may need to build application materials, attend events,[practice interviews](https://www.hiration.com/blog/ai-mock-interview-student-readiness-higher-ed/) , act on feedback, explore options, network, and apply for opportunities.


Introducing those expectations before enrollment gives students a more realistic understanding of how career support works.


## How Can Career Services Stay Present Between Admission and Enrollment?


Career Services should use the period between admission and arrival to turn awareness into a small number of clear next steps.


This does not require a large[pre-arrival career program](https://www.hiration.com/blog/orientation-week-career-programming-services-higher-ed/) . The goal is simply to prevent career support from disappearing after the admissions conversation.


Depending on the institution, Career Services might introduce:


- how students will access career resources
- important internship or recruiting timelines
- career exploration tools
- an initial resume or professional-profile activity
- first-term career events
- any career preparation expected during the first semester


This matters most when recruiting or internship timelines begin early.


If prospective students hear extensively about career support during recruitment but then receive no career-related communication until orientation, the experience becomes disconnected.


Career Services can reduce that gap by giving admitted and deposited students one or two useful actions before they arrive.


## What Should the Admissions-to-Career-Services Handoff Look Like?


The handoff should give students a specific first action and make it obvious how to continue the career preparation introduced during admissions.


Simply telling students to “visit the Career Center” is too broad.


A stronger handoff might look like this:


Student stage What Career Services should introduce Student next step


Admitted Career preparation can begin before arrival Review available career resources


Deposited Career support will be part of the student experience Complete an initial exploration or profile activity


Pre-arrival Some career preparation starts early Identify interests or prepare a baseline resume


Orientation Career Services is now part of the student's support system Activate the relevant platform, attend an introduction, or complete the first activity


First weeks Continue the preparation already introduced Use resources and seek advisor support where needed


The exact activity will vary by institution. What matters is continuity.


If Admissions talked about resume support, students should know where to start once they enroll.


If internships featured heavily in recruitment conversations, students should know when internship preparation begins.


If[career exploration](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-exploration-advisor-framework-higher-ed/) was discussed, students should have an obvious way to continue it.


Career Services should not have to restart the career conversation from zero once students arrive.


From Recruitment to Enrollment: One Continuous Career Journey


## What Should Career Services Own, Influence, and Coordinate With Admissions?


Career Services should own the accuracy of career information and the student career-development experience, influence how those areas are described during recruitment, and coordinate the transition into career support after enrollment.


A practical division looks like this:


Career Services should own Career Services should influence Career Services should coordinate with Admissions


Career outcomes methodology and interpretation How career support is described Career messaging used in recruitment


Description of career services and resources How student expectations are framed Approved outcome claims


Career-specific guidance How employer and salary information is presented Admitted-student career communication


Student career-development experience When career preparation is introduced Admissions-to-Career-Services handoff


Admissions still owns the prospective-student relationship.


Career Services does not need to become part of every recruitment conversation.


Its role is to make sure the career information being used is accurate, the support being described matches reality, and students know what happens next once they enroll.


When that partnership works, prospective students get a clearer picture of career outcomes before making an enrollment decision, and enrolled students experience continuity instead of having to relearn what Career Services is and how to use it.


## Conclusion


Career Services does not need to become an extension of Admissions. It needs to make sure the career story prospective students hear is accurate, specific, and connected to what they will actually experience after enrollment.


That means giving Admissions reliable outcomes data and context, clarifying how career support should be described, setting expectations about student participation, and creating a clear handoff into career preparation.
